answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB) resources live under the Microsoft.DocumentDB provider. The account resource type is: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (child resources include Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases and Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbCollections).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer:
Use the built-in Azure CLI group az cosmosdb (core CLI). Examples: 
- Create an account: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus --default-consistency-level Session
- Manage MongoDB resources under az cosmosdb mongodb (e.g. az cosmosdb mongodb database create ...). This is part of the core az cosmosdb command group, not a separate extension in normal installs.

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer:
Bicep/ARM: the main account resource is Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. MongoDB DB and collection child resource types are Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases and Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbCollections.
Terraform (azurerm): azurerm_cosmosdb_account for the account; azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database and azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection for MongoDB databases and collections.

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer:
Typical Cosmos DB (MongoDB API) connection string (SQL-style, TLS required):
mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false&appName=@<account>@
Notes: host suffix is <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com, port 10255 (TLS). username is usually the Mongo user or the account user often formatted like user@account; ssl=true and replicaSet=globaldb and retrywrites=false are commonly required options.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB bills throughput in Request Units (RU/s). For the MongoDB API you provision throughput as RUs (per-collection or database) or use autoscale (auto-provisioned RU). There is also a serverless option for certain Cosmos accounts/regions; the primary billing/factoring model for production workloads is provisioned RU/s (or autoscale RUs).

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Data-plane (MongoDB API) clients authenticate using MongoDB-style username/password (SCRAM) credentials backed by Cosmos account keys or Mongo users. The typical pattern is username/password in the Mongo connection string (password often the primary key or a MongoDB user password). Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) is used for the management plane (az CLI, ARM, SDK) but Entra ID is not supported as a direct MongoDB wire-protocol authentication method for data-plane connections (i.e., drivers do not authenticate to the Mongo endpoint with Azure AD tokens).

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB API use the official MongoDB drivers (e.g., pymongo for Python). There is no separate special 'Cosmos DB Mongo driver' — use standard pymongo/MongoClient against the Cosmos Mongo endpoint. For management/administration you can use the Azure Cosmos SDK/az CLI which are service-specific.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: To my knowledge Azure Cosmos DB's MongoDB API does not provide native vector search indexes (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN) as first-class index types the way MongoDB Atlas Vector Search does. Therefore there is no service-specific create-vector-index command for Cosmos; vector search would rely on external search services (e.g., Azure Cognitive Search) or application-side approximate-nearest-neighbour libraries. (No native CREATE INDEX ... USING HNSW command exists in Cosmos Mongo API.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text search for Cosmos DB workloads is typically done by integrating Azure Cognitive Search (indexing Cosmos data into an Azure Cognitive Search index) or by using an external search system. The MongoDB API does not have an Atlas-style integrated full-text/hybrid vector search; integrate with Azure Cognitive Search or a dedicated search system for hybrid text+vector search.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API exposes a Mongo wire protocol compatibility layer and has historically supported several Mongo server versions (3.2 / 3.6 / 4.0 / 4.2 and later additions in newer accounts). Exact supported server/wire versions depend on account configuration. Common Mongo features that are limited or not supported include: server-side JavaScript (eval), some aggregation stages/operators differences, full MongoDB changeStreams historically not supported (Cosmos has its own change feed), and some multi-document transaction features or advanced sharding semantics may differ. Verify exact supported server version for your account before relying on a very new MongoDB server feature.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: For Cosmos DB core API you can use the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator locally. The Emulator primarily targets the SQL (Core) API and has limited cross-API support. For MongoDB API development use a local MongoDB server (official Docker image) listening on the standard port 27017, e.g. docker run -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo -d mongo:6.0. When testing against an actual Cosmos Mongo account use the account's mongodb endpoint (port 10255 with TLS).

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB provides a Change Feed for the Core API which can be used to capture data changes; the MongoDB API historically did not support native MongoDB changeStreams in the same way as a MongoDB server. So, for MongoAPI you generally use Cosmos change feed patterns or the management plane features instead of native Mongo changeStreams. No special per-collection toggle is normally required to use Cosmos change feed beyond having data in a partitioned container with throughput; check account docs for required settings.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: I expect a service-specific MCP server (documentdb or cosmosdb) provides data-plane inspection tools for Cosmos DB (indexes, query plans). The general Azure MCP server handles management-plane operations, but for Mongo-specific data-plane tools you would use the documentdb/cosmosdb MCP server endpoints. (I am not certain of the exact MCP server name/version in your environment.)

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Microsoft originally launched a proprietary document database service named DocumentDB. Later the service was rebranded and expanded as Azure Cosmos DB, which now exposes multiple APIs (SQL/Core - the original DocumentDB API, MongoDB API, Cassandra API, Gremlin, Table). The open-source 'DocumentDB' projects are distinct; Cosmos DB is Microsoft's managed proprietary engine that implements a DocumentDB-style API and multiple wire protocol compatibilities (including MongoDB).

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: The service runs on Microsoft's proprietary Cosmos DB engine which implements compatibility layers for various APIs (including MongoDB). That means application code using standard MongoDB drivers will usually work, but some Mongo server features/behaviours differ or are unsupported (see differences in aggregation, transactions, change streams and server-side JS). Plan for these API differences and test queries against the Cosmos account.

answers.question: What connection details and env var will the sample rely on?
answers.answer: Read the MongoDB connection URI at runtime from DOCUMENTDB_URI environment variable. Expect a standard Cosmos Mongo URI like: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false&appName=@<account>@. Do not write the actual secret to disk; use a .env.example placeholder.

answers.question: Which database and collection names will the sample create and use?
answers.answer: Use the database sample_customer_360_18. Collections to create/use: customers (customer profiles), workflows (batch run logs), deduped_customers (merged canonical profiles), and enrichments (third-party signals). Create indexes such as customers.create_index([('customer_id', 1)], unique=True) and customers.create_index([('email', 1)]) via pymongo.

answers.question: Which client library and example connection code will the sample use in Python?
answers.answer: Use pymongo. Example: from pymongo import MongoClient; client = MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI'], tls=True); db = client['sample_customer_360_18']; customers = db['customers']. This is the library the orchestration and agents will use to read/write documents.

answers.question: What index and query patterns will the sample rely on for deduplication and workflow logging?
answers.answer: Create an index on canonical identifiers and common match keys: customers.create_index([('customer_id', 1)], unique=True); customers.create_index([('normalized_email', 1)]); customers.create_index([('phone_normalized', 1)]). Workflows collection will use an index on run_id and timestamp: workflows.create_index([('run_id', 1)], unique=True); workflows.create_index([('started_at', -1)]).

answers.question: How will LLM-assisted matching be integrated (auth and storage expectations)?
answers.answer: LLM calls are made from the orchestration layer (not via the DB). The dedup agent will store candidate pairs and LLM match decisions as documents in a dedupe_jobs collection with fields {pair_id, left_id, right_id, score, verdict, evidence}. No special DB-side auth; use the same DOCUMENTDB_URI connection and standard pymongo writes. Keep LLM prompt/evidence trimmed before storing to avoid logging secrets.
